https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/politics/w.title: Who are 'The Five Families'? All the Tory rebel groups threatening misery for Rishi Sunak
https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/politics/w.text:
Rishi Sunak is struggling to quash a major Tory rebellion as he attempts to revive his stalled Rwanda deportation scheme.
The Prime Minister is trying to rush through emergency legislation to overcome the Supreme Court's objections to his plan to ship migrants to the African country. MPs are drawing battle lines in a two-day Commons debate over the Safety of Rwanda Bill, with crunch votes expected tomorrow.
Backbench plotters from different Conservative joined forces at its first Commons stage before Christmas to turn the screws on the Prime Minister. Dubbing themselves "The Five Families", in a nod to the mafia in the US, the rebels threatened to torpedo the legislation but in the end settled on abstaining in the crunch vote.
It meant a stay of execution for the PM but he now faces a nightmare as rebels made it clear they could sink the Bill unless he caves to their demands. And Rwanda could be just the start as the emboldened right-wingers scent weakness. While Mr Sunak has a sizeable majority, only 29 Tories need to rebel in the Commons to derail the Government's plans.
Here we look at the Tory rebels making the Prime Minister's life a misery
The European Research Group (ERG) is a powerful caucus of right-wing Eurosceptics who made Theresa May's life a misery as she tried to get a deal with Brussels in 2018 and 2019. The ERG was highly influential on Tory policy during this period and a number of its members were given Government jobs, including Suella Braverman, Jacob Rees-Mogg and Steve Baker.
It's influence has waned since, particularly after Mr Baker, its former leader and top backbench organiser, entered Government. But it has returned to the fore to lobby the Government over immigration. Its current leader Mark Francois revived its so-called star chamber of lawyers to scrutinise the Rwanda Bill, who said it needed "significant amendments".
The newest rebel wing was only created in May but boasts around 25 members, including a number of influential Red Wall MPs. Its aim is to shift the party to the right, and its co-founders Miriam Cates and Danny Kruger have been vocal on tax cuts and social issues such as traditional family values.
It also takes a hard line on immigration, publishing a report earlier this year demanding a crackdown on temporary visas for care workers and a cap on refugee numbers. Ms Cates, who abstained on the vote, said the Rwanda Bill was "defective" and had too many loopholes to allow legal challenges.
Mr Kruger, the MP for Devizes, has made it clear he dislikes the Mafia associations. "I wish we weren't portrayed in these melodramatic terms," he told i news. "I don't think any of us are happy to be associated with the Mafia."
Dozens of Tories are members of this ERG-inspired group, which was created to give right-wingers a forum to co-ordinate pressure on the Government. The Common Sense Tories stand for "authentic Conservatism" and often wade into the culture wars, criticising Black Lives Matter and Extinction Rebellion protesters, as well as the National Trust for its work on slavery and colonialism.
The group has also weighed in against "nanny state" policies and took a dim view of Mr Sunak's plans to phase out smoking. Chairman Sir John Hayes is a former minister and a close ally of former Home Secretary Suella Braverman, and the group is hard line on both legal and illegal immigration.
Led by Carlisle MP John Stevenson, the NRG was formed to lobby for investment in the North of England after the party swelled its numbers in the Red Wall in 2019. The group, which has around 55 members including former minister Jake Berry, has spoken out on tax, devolution and called for a route map out of Covid restrictions in late 2020.
The NRG has a number of Brexiteers in its ranks and has also identified immigration as key electoral issue in its heartlands.
Allies of disaster PM Liz Truss set up this group after her 49-day stint in Downing Street to continue to push her economic policies. Chaired by former Cabinet minister Ranil Jayawardena, its 50-strong membership also includes Dame Priti Patel and ex-Cabinet Minister Simon Clarke.
The libertarian group mostly does what it says on the tin, pushing for tax cuts and deregulation called for by Ms Truss before her premiership dramatically unravelled.
The moderate "One Nation" group is the largest faction within the Tory party, with more than 100 members. Formed back in 2019 to oppose a no-deal Brexit, it is now led by Theresa May's former de facto deputy Damian Green.
Many of its members were prominent during David Cameron's time in Downing Street but have fallen out of favour since Brexit. However it does still have some influence in Government - as Justice Secretary Alex Chalk and Education Secretary Gillian Keegan both have top jobs. It is broadly supportive of Mr Sunak, partly because weakening him would open the door to a challenge from the right of the party.
This group is not among the "five families" as it takes a different stance on the Rwanda plan, arguing vocally against any moves that break international law. They have previously been critical of calls to override the European Convention on Human Rights - which has been suggested by some right-wing MPs.
